Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

soilKey 0.9.293 (2026-10-28)

New Zealand Soil Classification: the 15 orders

A new, experimental and opt-in system: the New Zealand Soil Classification, 4th edition (Manaaki Whenua - Landcare Research 2026), read from its Quarto source of 7 October 2026. classify_nzsc4() keys a pedon to the 15 orders of the Key to Soil Orders (Organic, Gley, Ultic, Podzol, Allophanic, Pumice, Melanic, Semiarid, Oxidic, Granular, Pallic, Brown, Anthropic, Recent and Raw Soils); make_nzsc4_example() gives one example profile per order. Groups and subgroups follow; the Cryic Soils of the appendix are not keyed. classify_all(systems = "nzsc") runs it.

The diagnostics read the New Zealand horizon notation (Bw, Bt, Bg, Bh, Bs, Bo, Bx, Bw(g), the pans Bhm, Bsm, Blm, Bfm, CR, an e prefix for anthropic soil material), moist colours, texture groups, pH, P retention, bulk density, volcanic glass, coarse fragments and their origin, structure and clay coatings, and the New Zealand field tests, as five new horizon attributes: naf_test (reactive aluminium), childs_test, sensitivity_class, fluidity_class and stickiness. From the site: drainage class, parent material (Melanic Soils), human truncation and an overthickened A horizon (the note to the key).

Three readings are Hugo’s decisions: a reductimorphic horizon in a designated profile is read from its notation (g, r, or peat), as pale B horizons of Pallic Soils have low chroma without being reduced; a measured P retention decides allophanic soil material, the field tests standing in only when it is not measured; and a reductimorphic horizon that reaches the base of the B horizon meets the depth condition of the Gley Soils. The other readings are in inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml. WRB, SiBCS, USDA, Canadian and Australian results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.292 (2026-10-27)

Australian classification: the families

classify_asc3(include_family = TRUE) now places a soil in the family classes of its order and writes them after the name, as the book does: “Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol; thick, non-gravelly, loamy/clayey, deep”. The new classify_asc3_family() returns each criterion as a FamilyAttribute with its code (YY when the data cannot decide the class, ZZ when no class of the order fits); the result keeps them in trace$family, trace$family_label and trace$family_code. classify_all(include_family = TRUE) passes the option on when the Australian key is run. Without the option nothing changes.

The criteria are those of each order page: the thickness of the A1, or of the whole A in the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols and in the Kurosolic, Sodosolic and Chromosolic Hydrosols (the book’s general rule, where the order pages disagree); gravel (2-60 mm) of the surface and A1, the larger of the two estimates; the field texture of the A1 and the most clayey one of the B; soil depth (to rock, a cemented pan or saprolite; otherwise to the C under the B, or the depth described in a soil without a B); and water repellence. The Vertosols use laboratory clay, the Calcarosols the depth of the Bk, the Arenosols and Rudosols the surface soil, the Organosols their organic materials. The Anthroposols and the tidal Hydrosols have none. The classes and the criteria of each order are in inst/rules/asc3/families.yaml, the readings in readings.yaml.

Two horizon attributes: gravel_pct (gravel-sized fragments) and water_repellence. The NatSoil reader fills them, with the coarse fragments of the ground surface and the surveyors’ family codes, and benchmark_natsoil(family = TRUE) compares each criterion. On the NatSoil profiles whose order agrees, the decided classes agree with the surveyors for 85 % of the thicknesses, 87 % of the A1 textures, 97 % of the B textures, 83 % of the depths and 75 % of the gravel classes. The Vertosol clay classes are mostly undecided: only 29 of 291 NatSoil Vertosols have laboratory clay.

No order, suborder, great group or subgroup changes on NatSoil. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.291 (2026-10-27)

Australian classification: subgroups of the Rudosolic and Tenosolic Hydrosols

The Hydrosol page points the Rudosolic and Tenosolic great groups of the Redoxic and Oxyaquic Hydrosols to the subgroup lists of the Rudosols and Tenosols. classify_asc3() now keys such a soil, apart from wetness, through the Rudosol or Tenosol suborders, and takes the list of the suborder it keys to: “Basic, Rudosolic, Oxyaquic Hydrosol”. Those lists are the same for every great group of a suborder, so the soil is keyed to the suborder only. Apart from wetness, the Hypersalic Rudosol suborder is read by its salinity alone (its other conditions, no water table and no mottling, are wetness). A suborder with no list (Shelly, Carbic) gives no subgroup. A suborder left undecided before the one assigned makes the subgroup provisional only when it would lead to another list. The Salic Rudosolic and Tenosolic Hydrosols keep the Salic list.

The rules name these great groups under subgroups_from in the Hydrosol subgroup file, with site fields set for the walk only (.apart_from_wetness); load_rules() reads such blocks, the rule validator checks them, and the key walks the other order as the main key would, only as deep as the choice of list needs. The walk shows in the trace as a phase of its own (“suborders, as a Rudosol”).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles only the five that key to these great groups change: two get a subgroup, two stay undecided for lack of data, and one fits none of the three Rudosol subgroups (exactly half of its soil is strongly acid). Nothing else changes, at any level. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.290 (2026-10-26)

Australian classification: carbonate segregations recorded as none

A horizon whose carbonate segregations are recorded as none (0 %), with no effervescence or CaCO3 recorded, was left undecided by the test of “calcareous”, although the same horizon with nothing recorded is read by its pH (a pHw below 7.0 is not calcareous, as free carbonate holds the pH higher). A recorded 0 % of segregations says nothing of the fine-earth carbonate, so the pH rule now applies to it too. Found in the review of 0.9.289.

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles no order or suborder changes, and 32 more orders are decided (1,305, at 74.5 %). 98 great groups change, nearly all to Eutrophic, which needs B and BC horizons that are not calcareous; the great groups that agree with the survey go from 1,076 to 1,140 and the subgroups from 499 to 555. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.289 (2026-10-26)

Australian classification: subgroups of the Hydrosols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() keys the subgroups of the last four orders, so every order that has great groups now keys its subgroups. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and great groups, nor the subgroups of the ten orders keyed before.

  • Hydrosols: Fibric, Hemic and Sapric for the Histic-Hypersulfidic and Histic-Hyposulfidic Intertidal Hydrosols; Episulfidic-Petrocalcic, Episulfidic and Petrocalcic for the Salic ones; 40 subgroups for the Redoxic and Oxyaquic ones, without the acidic subgroups for the Kurosolic great groups and without the sodic and natric ones for the Sodosolic, as the page says. The page sends the Rudosolic and Tenosolic great groups to the Rudosol and Tenosol lists; that is not keyed yet, and they keep the great group’s name.
  • Arenosols: 13 subgroups for the Chernic, Bleached and coloured suborders, read over the upper 1.0 m of the profile; the carbonate great groups take the list without Humose-Calcareous, Melanic-Calcareous and Calcareous, as the page says.
  • Rudosols: Acidic, Basic and Calcareous, read over the soil above any rock, pan or buried soil; for every suborder but the Shelly and Carbic. The Hypergypsic, Lutic and Stratic Rudosols have no great groups, and their subgroups follow the suborder (“Basic, Lutic Rudosol”): the hierarchical key skips a level only when the next one has a list named by the exact path.
  • Tenosols: one list per suborder (4, 9, 6, 3, 12, 7 and 13 subgroups): chernic horizons with the acidity and carbonate of the B, the A2 or the solum; Subpeaty, Subhumose, Submelacic and Submelanic (every requirement but the thickness); Lithocalcic, Supracalcic and Hypercalcic for the Calcenic Tenosols, read on the Calcenic horizon.
  • Readings decided with Hugo: the Salic Hydrosols take only the three subgroups listed; in the coloured Tenosols Basic is read as no part of the solum calcareous (the page’s “the A2 horizon” read as a misprint); in the Chernic Tenosols “the B horizon (if present)” with no B fails.
  • benchmark_natsoil() reads the survey’s subgroup of a suborder with no great groups from its great-group column.
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (57).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, 195 of the 414 profiles of these four orders that reach a subgroup list get a subgroup (75 decided). Only 20 can be compared with the survey (5 agree): most survey labels of these orders use older codes, and many profiles stop at a great group the survey does not give.

soilKey 0.9.288 (2026-10-26)

Australian classification: subgroups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and Organosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() keys the subgroups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and Organosols, one list per order as the order pages give them (43, 12, 15 and 8 subgroups). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and great groups, nor the subgroups of the six orders keyed before.

  • Vertosols: the acid sulfate subgroups as for the acid sulfate great groups; Salic as for the Salic Hydrosols; Duric and Petrocalcic; the upper 0.1 m of the solum sodic (Episodic, by its weighted average ESP); the upper 0.5 m of the solum and the solum below it strongly acid, calcareous, mottled or with an ESP of 15 or more (Epiacidic, Endocalcareous, Epihypersodic and their combinations); Magnesic over the B. The solum is read as described, pans left out, rows of unknown role and horizons of unknown depth tried every way they may go.
  • Calcarosols: Melanic, Vertic, Subplastic and Gypsic; Epibasic and Hypervescent as for the Calsilic Arenosols; Supravescent; Epihypersodic and Endohypersodic; Ceteric for the others. The Carbonatic Calcarosols take the list without Supravescent and Hypervescent, as the page says they are not required there.
  • Podosols: a strongly or weakly coherent B (Parapanic, Fragic), a densipan in the A2 (Densic), a thin ironpan in or under the B (Placic), a siliceous pan under the B, a ferric horizon in the B, with the peaty, humose, melacic and melanic combinations.
  • Organosols: what the organic materials directly overlie (Lithic, Paralithic, Marly, Rudaceous, Modic), a thin ironpan below them, and layers of unconsolidated mineral material within or below them (Terric within 0.8 m, Regolithic below).
  • The examples of the four orders key to a subgroup (“Endocalcareous, Self-mulching, Black Vertosol”).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (56).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, 424 of the 533 profiles keyed to these four orders with a great group get a subgroup. Of the 347 whose order, suborder and great group agree with the survey and whose survey gives a subgroup of the key, 261 get one and 113 (43 %) the survey’s (Vertosols 100 of 239). Nearly every Vertosol subgroup stays provisional: the Sulfuric subgroup needs the pH of the upper 1.5 m, and the Sulfidic one a sulfide test, rarely recorded (read as absent, a test not done would decide 11 more Vertosols and leave the agreement unchanged).

soilKey 0.9.287 (2026-10-26)

Australian classification: subgroups of the Dermosols, Kandosols and Ferrosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() keys the subgroups of the Dermosols, Kandosols and Ferrosols, one list per order as the order pages give them (33, 29 and 14 subgroups). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • These pages read the B2 horizon where the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols read the B2t: mottled, whole coloured, and strongly acid (Acidic, Humose-Acidic, Melanic-Acidic, Ferric-Acidic, Manganic-Acidic, Acidic-Sodic, Bleached-Acidic, Acidic-Mottled: the major part of the B2 with a pHw below 5.5, or a pHCa below 4.6 without pHw).
  • New in the Kandosols: an argic or a bauxitic horizon within the B (Argic, Bauxitic). New in the Ferrosols: Snuffy (an A horizon with a very fine granular structure, peds under 2 mm, and a weak or very weak dry strength), and Sodic read on the lower part of the B2, as printed.
  • The Kandosol page says the acidic subgroups are not required for the calcareous great groups: the Hypocalcic, Lithocalcic, Supracalcic, Hypercalcic and Calcic Kandosols take the list without them, as the Natric Kurosols take theirs without the Sodic ones.
  • The examples of the three orders record organic C, mottles and the CEC, and key to a subgroup (“Haplic, Eutrophic, Brown Dermosol”).
  • The dark horizon of the Chernic suborders (melacic or melanic) is now decided over every extent it may have, as the subgroups read it since 0.9.286. Before, a horizon 0.2 m thick in its surely black rows was read on those rows only, though rows that may be black below could change its major part, and a gap in the record directly above the first row that may not be black was not counted as possibly black. Such a gap may likewise be organic material (the peaty horizon, where the mineral surface lies) or fusic material (Fusic Anthroposols); where the mineral surface may lie at more than one depth, a verdict holds only when it holds at each. Over a clear or abrupt textural B, a row of unknown role between two A horizons is now read as an A horizon (before, as not black).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (55).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders and great groups do not change. The Chernic test becomes undecided on five profiles, where a suborder was already provisional, and decided on one: a Tenosol whose A1 (17.6 % organic C) may or may not be organic material gives a humose horizon either way, and is now Chernic. Of the 799 profiles keyed to these three orders with a great group, 549 get a subgroup. Of the 278 whose order, suborder and great group agree with the survey and whose survey gives a subgroup of the key, 213 get one and 113 (53 %) the survey’s (Dermosols 32 of 65, Kandosols 80 of 137, Ferrosols 1 of 11). Most of the others stop at Humose-Mottled, which needs organic C in the upper 0.2 m. The Ferrosol disagreements come from one survey whose profiles have 5 to 9 % organic C (combustion, a method the glossary names) at the surface, a humose horizon, but were surveyed Haplic or Acidic.

soilKey 0.9.286 (2026-10-26)

Australian classification: subgroups of the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys a fourth level, the subgroups, for the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols; the other orders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and great groups, but their names now take the book’s form.

  • The names follow the general form the book gives, “Subgroup, Great Group, Suborder Order”: “Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol”. The great groups carry the same comma (“Eutrophic, Red Chromosol”; before, “Eutrophic Red Chromosol”).
  • One list per order, as the order pages give it, applied under every great group of the order: chernic horizons (peaty, humose, melacic, melanic), a conspicuously bleached A2, a B with at least 0.3 m of vertic properties, ferric and manganic horizons within the solum, the lower part of the B sodic, the B2t mottled or whole coloured, a reticulate horizon below the B2t, a gypsic horizon in the B or BC, a siliceous pan in the lower A or upper B, Magnesic, base status, the carbonate classes and Effervescent, combined as the lists combine them (Bleached-Sodic, Mottled-Sodic, Ferric-Sodic and so on).
  • The hierarchical key finds a list for every class under a part of the path (“CH-*“) and writes a name on the name of the class above (”Bleached, {parent}“); other systems do not change.
  • benchmark_natsoil() reports the subgroups ($subgroups).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (54).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders, suborders and great groups do not change. Of the 560 profiles keyed to these three orders with a great group, 294 get a subgroup. Of the 173 whose order, suborder and great group agree with the survey and whose survey gives a subgroup of the key, 79 get one and 37 (47 %) the survey’s; most of the others stop at Humose, which needs organic C in the upper 0.2 m, rarely measured. The disagreements checked are survey practice: B horizons of heavy clay with many slickensides and lenticular peds surveyed Haplic rather than Vertic.

soilKey 0.9.285 (2026-10-24)

Australian classification: great groups of the Hydrosols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys the great groups of every order that has them (the Anthroposols have none in the text). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change; three Australian orders change on NatSoil, because an AC horizon is now part of the solum (see below).

  • Hydrosols: the acid sulfate groups as for the Organosols (with Histic-Hypersulfidic and Histic-Hyposulfidic), then by suborder: Histic, Faunic, Epicalcareous and the particle-size groups for the tidal and subaqueous soils; Gypsic, Halic, Epicalcareous, Mottled and Haplic for the Supratidal and Hypersalic; and for the Extratidal, Salic, Redoxic and Oxyaquic, Petroferric and the order the soil would key to apart from wetness (Calcarosolic to Rudosolic).
  • Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols: what the soil directly overlies (hard rock, saprolite, marl, unconsolidated material, a red-brown hardpan, a calcrete pan, ferricrete, a siliceous pan, a reticulate horizon, coquina), “overlie” being read as “directly overlie”; ferric, bauxitic and manganic horizons; gypsic and argic horizons; Inceptic (a C/B), Tephric, Andic, Gritty, Gravic, Halic and Subhalic; the carbonate classes; Kandic, Tenic and Palic Arenosols; Epibasic and Hypervescent Calsilic Arenosols; Arenic Tenosols; Colluvic, Fluvic and Lithosolic Clastic Rudosols. In the Arenosols hard layers count only below 1.0 m.
  • Nodules not recorded are read as absent (more than 20 % of nodules shows); this also applies to the Sesqui-Nodular Tenosols, which read them as unknown since 0.9.282. A gritty feel, heavy minerals, halite and gypsum not recorded are absent too.
  • What the soil directly overlies, shared with the Calcarosols: a C or D horizon of unrecorded origin is no longer read as possibly hard rock, nor is sandy material read as possibly marl (Lithic and Marly Calcarosols included); a cemented layer that is no pan may still be rock, while one whose origin names saprolite is saprolite; a horizon recorded as a pan that makes up the layer (ferricrete, calcrete and the like) is a pan whatever its designation, and ferricrete or silcrete named by the layer or rock origin counts; an AC horizon is part of the solum, which moves three NatSoil profiles from Tenosols or Rudosols to Vertosols and Calcarosols, all three now as surveyed.
  • New horizon attributes: manganiferous_nodules_pct, gypsum_visible_pct, halite_visible_pct, gritty, heavy_minerals_pct. The NatSoil reader fills the first three from the segregations, counting only those recorded as nodules or segregations of that kind (NaN where the recorded classes leave the amount on either side of the limit, which the key reads as undecided).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (52).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, three orders change, all three now as surveyed (1,273 decided, 74.8 % of them agreeing), and 51 fewer suborders are provisional, from the Sesqui-Nodular reading. Of the 3,536 profiles keyed to these four orders, 398 get a great group; most stop at the suborder, which is itself undecided for many Tenosols, and the Hydrosols wait on the sulfide test. Only 42 can be compared with the survey (order and suborder agreeing, a great group of the key): 21 get the survey’s great group. Most Tenosol labels use the suborder codes of the editions before 2021.

soilKey 0.9.284 (2026-10-24)

Australian classification: great groups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and Organosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys the great groups of four more orders, ten in all. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and the great groups of 0.9.283.

  • Vertosols, by the surface: Self-mulching (a moderately or strongly self-mulching surface in the site record, as the text asks that the group be used only when the condition is not in doubt), Epipedal (a pedal A, blocky or polyhedral), Crusty (a surface crusty horizon over pedal clay: a surface crust in the site record, or a surface horizon 30 mm thick or less that is massive or weakly structured), Massive (massive or weak blocky), Peaty. The site record is read item by item, negations included; a thin organic layer at the top is passed over.
  • Calcarosols: Duric and Petrocalcic (a pan directly under the soil), Rendic (the A directly over a Bk of more than 80 % soft carbonate, Hypercalcic only), Argic (clay lamellae in the B), Pedal, and what the soil directly overlies (Lithic, Paralithic, Marly, Regolithic), read from the designation, the layer or rock origin and any pan; a C of unrecorded origin, a description that stops at the base of the solum, or a row of unknown role that may be part of it, leaves them undecided.
  • Podosols, by the kinds of Podosol B in the designations (Bs, Bhs, Bh, and a Basi under a Bh), with each suborder’s own list as printed, and Pipey where an A2 has a tongued boundary. The NatSoil reader now keeps the boundary shape (boundary_topography).
  • Organosols: Folic (freely drained, organic materials as in Definition (ii)), Sulfuric, Sulfidic and the groups that replace them only with the evidence (Hypersulfidic, Hyposulfidic; no monosulfidic test is recorded), then Calcareous, Basic, Acidic. The upper 1.5 m includes buried horizons, and a part of it not described may hold acid sulfate material; sulfidic material not tested leaves the great group provisional.
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (48).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, of the 465 of these orders whose order and suborder agree and whose survey gives a great group of the key, 75.5 % get the survey’s great group, and 76.4 % of the 301 decided (the Vertosols: 324 of 418, and 220 of the 281 decided). Several surveys record the crust of a Crusty Vertosol as a thin A11 over a pedal A12, which is read as the text describes it. The Calcarosols and Organosols stay provisional for want of data: the suborder or what lies under the solum for the first, the sulfide test for the second.

soilKey 0.9.283 (2026-10-23)

Australian classification: great groups of the Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols, Ferrosols, Dermosols and Kandosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys a third level, the great groups, for the six orders with a B horizon of their own; the name is the great group’s (“Eutrophic Red Chromosol”). The other orders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders and suborders.

  • Pans in or under the B: Duric (red-brown hardpan), Petroferric (ferricrete), Petrocalcic (a calcrete pan under a B that is not calcareous), Placic (thin ironpan), from a new attribute pan_type (NatSoil records it, “none” included) or the designation (km, sm, qm, cm). A pan the record does not show is absent, as the order reads hard layers; a cemented layer of unknown kind leaves it undecided.
  • The B2t or B2: Pedaric, Subplastic, Magnesic (exchangeable Ca/Mg below 0.1), Natric, base status (Dystrophic, Mesotrophic, Eutrophic, from the exchangeable bases and clay, the clay range of the field texture where no lab clay), the Sodosol ESP classes with their Mottled forms, and the carbonate classes as for the Calcarosols.
  • Ferrosol Calcareous, Kandosol Leptic, Mellic and Andic.
  • Hypocalcic now needs some carbonate in the solum (the class is of weakly calcareous soils); this does not change the Calcarosols.
  • The hierarchical key finds the list under a class by the codes of the path to it (“CH-AA”), since the Australian suborder codes repeat from order to order; other systems do not change.
  • benchmark_natsoil() reports the great groups ($great_groups).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (44).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, of the 2,160 of these orders whose order and suborder agree and whose survey gives a great group of the key, 21.6 % get the survey’s great group, and 80.6 % of the 98 decided. Most stay provisional for want of laboratory data: exchangeable Ca and Mg (Magnesic, before the base status classes), the bases and clay, mottles (the Mottled Sodosols) and, for the Kandosols, the porosity the Mellic great group asks.

soilKey 0.9.282 (2026-10-23)

Australian classification: the suborders of the Anthroposols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys the suborders of all fifteen orders. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders.

  • Peaty, humose, melacic and melanic horizons (Chernic suborders), as the glossary defines them: organic C against clay for the humose horizon; black moist colour, a dry value of 5 or less, pH and structure for the melacic and melanic ones. Without organic C or a dry colour they are undecided.
  • The conspicuously bleached A2: an e (not a j) in the Australian notation, or the dry colour of the glossary (80 % bleached: mottles not recorded leave it undecided).
  • Leptic suborders: rock, a hard layer or a calcrete pan, or a C horizon of saprolite, with its top within 0.5 m; a C of unrecorded origin, or a description that stops at 0.5 m or above, is undecided.
  • Arenosols: Hypergypsic, Hypersalic (EC of a 1:5 extract above 2 dS/m, no water table, no mottles), Chernic, Carbonatic, Calsilic, Stratic, Bleached, then the colour of the upper 1.0 m of the profile.
  • Rudosols: Hypergypsic, Hypersalic, Shelly, Carbic, Leptic, Arenic (loose or weakly coherent sands), Lutic, Stratic, Clastic (gravelly).
  • Tenosols: Chernic-Leptic, Chernic, Sesqui-Nodular (a ferric or bauxitic horizon over more than half of the solum), Calcenic, Bleached-Leptic, Leptic, Bleached, then the colour of the upper 0.5 m of the profile.
  • Anthroposols: the kind of human-made material, from the layer origin.
  • A soil with no salinity record (no EC, no saline surface) is read as not highly saline; shells, carbic materials and fusic material the record does not mention are read as absent, as for the Hydrosol settings.
  • New horizon attributes ec_1to5_dS_m, strength_dry, strength_moist, ped_size_max_mm, ferric_nodules_pct, bauxitic_nodules_pct.
  • load_natsoil_pedons() reads them (EC method 3A1, strength classes, ped size, nodules from the segregations). Abundance classes are now added as ranges, each class strictly between its limits, so two records of 2-10 % and 10-20 % make 12-30 % (undecided at 20 %); before, their middles were added. This also applies to the soft and hard carbonate of 0.9.281.
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (39).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders are as before (43.9 %, 1,270 decided at 74.8 %). Of the 3,691 profiles of the fifteen orders whose order agrees and whose survey gives a 3rd-edition suborder, 75.9 % get the survey’s suborder, and 95.7 % of the 679 decided. Rudosols: 20 of 61, and the 10 decided agree; Arenosols 1 of 12 and Tenosols 15 of 222, none decided. Most Tenosols stay provisional because the organic C of the upper 0.2 m, the dry colours, the nodules or the origin of a shallow C horizon are not recorded; many surveyed Leptic Tenosols are described below 0.5 m with no rock, and the text does not make them leptic.

soilKey 0.9.281 (2026-10-22)

Australian classification: suborders of the Organosols, Podosols, Hydrosols and Calcarosols (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys the suborders of eleven of the fifteen orders. The four added here are read from the order pages and the glossary; the suborders of the Anthroposols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders.

  • Organosols: the kind of peat (fibric, hemic, sapric) with the greatest thickness; when kinds tie, the most decomposed (the Comment). The kind comes from the squeeze test of the glossary, then the rubbed fibre content, a peat field texture or an Oi, Oe or Oa designation.
  • Podosols: the saturation of the B horizon, from its days of saturation or from the drainage class. Rapidly drained is Aeric (the suborders define free drainage so); moderately well and imperfectly drained are Semiaquic; very poorly drained is Aquic; a well drained site stays undecided between Aeric and Semiaquic. Sulfuric material (at least 15 cm, pH below 4 with jarosite or hypersulfidic material below) and hypersulfidic material (incubation test) as the glossary defines them; without the test they are undecided.
  • Hydrosols: the setting of the soil from the site record (tidal zone, inland water, landform, a saline surface). A setting the record does not mention is read as absent, as the order key already reads tidal flooding. Then Redoxic (more than half of the profile mottled: more than 10 % distinct or prominent mottles) or Oxyaquic (more than half whole coloured).
  • Calcarosols: Hypergypsic (gypsum over 50 % in the solum; read as absent when no gypsum is recorded), Carbonatic (more than 40 % fine-earth carbonate in the upper 0.1 m), Hypocalcic, then the carbonate classes of a calcareous horizon (Bk, BCk or 10 % or more carbonate segregations): Lithocalcic, Supracalcic, Hypercalcic, Calcic.
  • New horizon attributes carbonate_soft_pct and carbonate_hard_pct (visual soft and hard pedogenic carbonate); mottle_contrast is now read by the ASC too.
  • load_natsoil_pedons() reads the landform pattern, mottles (abundance and contrast) and the soft and hard carbonate of the segregations and calcrete fragments. Where a segregation of unknown form or a fragment of unknown lithology leaves the amount spanning two carbonate classes, it is unknown.
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (30).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders are as before (43.9 %, 1,270 decided at 74.8 %). Of the 3,396 profiles of the eleven orders whose order agrees and whose survey gives a 3rd-edition suborder, 81.4 % get the survey’s suborder, and 95.7 % of the 669 decided. For the four orders added here: Organosols 4 of 10 (the 4 decided agree), Podosols 27 of 48 (26 of the 33 decided), Hydrosols 14 of 49 (6 of the 7 decided), Calcarosols 33 of 175 (the 2 decided agree). Most of these stay provisional for want of data in NatSoil: the kind of peat, the contrast of the mottles, the form of the carbonate segregations and laboratory carbonate.

soilKey 0.9.280 (2026-10-22)

Australian classification: the colour suborders (experimental)

classify_asc3() now keys the suborders of seven orders: the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols (the colour of the upper 0.2 m of the B2t), the Ferrosols, Dermosols and Kandosols (the upper 0.5 m of the B2) and the Vertosols (Aquic, then the colour of the upper 0.5 m of the solum). The name is the suborder’s (“Red Chromosol”); rsg_or_order keeps the order. The other suborders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • Colour classes as the ASC defines them (Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey, Black), from the moist matrix colour matched to the nearest chip; a colour half way between chips of different classes is of unknown class.
  • The dominant class covers more than half of the window; when no class does, the one with the largest share, as the surveyors read it (a tie is undecided).
  • Aquic Vertosols: saturation days of the upper 0.5 m, otherwise the drainage class as for the Hydrosols.
  • An imperfectly drained site (some horizons wet for several weeks, in the Field Handbook) now counts as not saturated for 2-3 months, for the Hydrosols and the Aquic Vertosols; before, it was undecided. No order changes, but more are decided. Organic materials keep their own limit: “saturated for long periods” is 30 days, as in Soil Taxonomy, whose definition the glossary adopts, so poorly and imperfectly drained sites stay undecided there.
  • benchmark_natsoil() also reports the suborders ($suborders).
  • The readings are in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (24).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles: the order agrees for 43.9 % as before, and 1,270 are now decided (was 1,052), 74.8 % in agreement. Of the 3,114 profiles of these seven orders whose order agrees and whose survey gives a suborder, 86.3 % get the survey’s suborder, and 96.6 % of the 623 decided.

soilKey 0.9.279 (2026-10-22)

Australian classification: the field texture first in the textural B (experimental)

The clear or abrupt textural B of classify_asc3() (Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols) now reads each horizon by its field texture grade, and by its lab clay only when it has none. The glossary gives the limits in clay “and/or” field texture and notes that where the two disagree the field texture may be the better guide to how the soil behaves; before, lab clay on both sides decided. The reading is in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml.

On the 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles with an ASC order, 255 change order: 104 of them now agree with the surveyors, 56 did before. Agreement goes from 43.4 % to 43.9 % (45.7 % counting the Arenosols as Tenosols or Rudosols), with 1,052 decided at 77.4 % (78.6 %). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.278 (2026-10-22)

NatSoil (CSIRO) as a benchmark for the Australian key (experimental)

NatSoil, the national soil site database of CSIRO, can now be read through its public API and used to check classify_asc3() against the orders the surveyors gave. The data are licensed per site, most under CC BY 4.0, and are not shipped: fetch_natsoil() saves them to a folder of your choice. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • fetch_natsoil() downloads every public site (about 150 pages) and then the horizons, samples and laboratory results of each licensed site with an ASC order (one request per site, about 9,800), with a pause between requests. Files already on disk are kept, so a run can be resumed. Sites not licensed for external use are skipped.
  • load_natsoil_pedons() turns the files into pedons: designations in the Australian notation, field texture grades, structure, moist and dry colours, slickensides, cracks, coarse fragments, calcareous segregations (records with only their nature are templates and are not read), pans, effervescence, plasticity type, the moisture when described, and laboratory pH, clay, exchangeable cations, CEC and effective CEC (whatever the extraction method, the “not recorded” methods included), ESP, organic C, free iron and carbonate. Samples count for the horizons they overlap, weighed by the overlap. A value below the detection limit (“<x”) is read as half the limit, unless the limit lies above one the keys read. The field pH stands in only where the laboratory has no pH, and the loss on ignition gives organic C only in peat. The site keeps the surveyors’ classification and confidence, the drainage class, the surface condition, coordinates, the licence and the citation.
  • benchmark_natsoil() compares the orders: agreement for all pedons and for the decided ones, by the surveyors’ confidence, recall by order, the confusion table and the first order left undecided. The surveys predate the 2021 Arenosols, so an Arenosol given to a surveyed Tenosol or Rudosol is also counted as agreement in the edition figures.
  • New horizon attribute esp_pct: the exchangeable sodium percentage as the laboratory reports it. classify_asc3() reads it for the sodic condition when exchangeable Na or the CEC is not given.

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles with an ASC order, the order agrees for 43.4 % (45.3 % counting the Arenosols as Tenosols or Rudosols); 1,045 are decided, with 77.8 % agreement (79.1 %); of the 450 decided with the surveyors’ highest confidence, 80.2 % agree (81.8 %).

soilKey 0.9.277 (2026-10-22)

Australian Soil Classification: the 15 orders (experimental)

classify_asc3() keys a pedon to the orders of the Australian Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Isbell and the National Committee on Soil and Terrain 2021), following the online version with its errata. It is the second national system on the registry (soilkey_systems(), alias asc) and, like the Canadian one, runs in classify_all() only when asked. Suborders, great groups, subgroups and families follow in later releases. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • The key reads the Australian horizon notation of the Field Handbook (A1, A2e, B21t, B3, Bhs, 2B2b …), and FAO or USDA designations by the role of each horizon (an E as an A2, a Bt as a B2t).
  • New horizon attributes: field_texture (the Field Handbook’s texture grades, such as SL, SCL or LMC, with + or -), subplasticity, soil_water_status (the moisture of the horizon when described) and effervescence_class. Where a limit is a texture grade the field texture decides and lab clay stands in; where it is in % clay, lab clay decides and the field texture stands in as the clay range of its grade.
  • The clear or abrupt textural B (Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols) reads the glossary’s clay figures, or its field-texture equivalents when lab clay is missing on either side of the boundary.
  • From the site the key reads the drainage class and tidal flooding (Hydrosols), a cracking surface condition (Vertosols) and the notation of the designations.
  • make_asc3_example() gives one small profile per order.
  • The choices where the text is silent are listed in inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml (21 readings). Two were settled on the survey data below: only a very poorly drained site counts as saturated for the Hydrosols (poorly drained is undecided), and the Vertosols’ cracks are not required in a solum described moist (the key’s “unless too moist”).

Checked against NatSoil (CSIRO, NatSoil v13, CC BY 4.0; the data are not shipped, and a reader will follow): of 9,698 profiles with an order from the surveys, 42.9 % get the same order (44.8 % counting the 2021 Arenosols against the Tenosols and Rudosols of earlier editions). 988 are decided, with no earlier order left open, and 78.6 % of them agree (80.1 %; 82.9 % of the 404 decided with the surveyors’ highest confidence). Most profiles stay provisional for missing data: the drainage class (Hydrosols), the designations (Podosols), the cracks (Vertosols), free iron (Ferrosols), carbonate records (Calcarosols) and exchangeable sodium (Sodosols).

soilKey 0.9.276 (2026-10-21)

Canadian classification: the colour of the Chernozemic great groups (experimental)

The key’s chroma limits for the Chernozemic great groups say “usually”. classify_cssc3() now reads them at two more places, each written down in inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml:

  • a dry value of exactly 3.5, the limit of both the Black Chernozems (“darker than 3.5”, Ch 5, p. 68) and the Dark Brown (3.5 to 4.5), is Black when the dry chroma is 1.5 or less, the chroma of the Black, unless an Ahe, Aej or Ae marks the eluviation of the Dark Gray, whose range holds 3.5;
  • in a cultivated soil, an Ap whose own dry chroma is 1.5 or less counts as the sign of eluviation of the Dark Gray Chernozems, whose Ahe the plough has mixed in (the key gives that Ap its own value limit, and Ch 5, p. 69, admits a mixed Ap); an Ahe, Aej or Ae in the profile still counts, and a buried one no longer does.

The colour means are rounded to the millionth before they meet a limit. On the NPDB scenario of 0.9.275, of the 348 Chernozems decided at the order level, 116 (was 92) get the survey’s great group, 84 of them (was 63) with the great group decided. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.275 (2026-10-21)

An NPDB scenario with the dry colour and the soil climate estimated (experimental)

The National Pedon Database of Canada records neither the dry colour of most A horizons nor the soil climate, which the Canadian key reads for the Chernozems (and the Gray Brown Luvisols and some subgroups). An optional scenario now estimates them, each as a range, and benchmark_npdb() classifies a pedon at the ends of its ranges, counting a class as decided only where they all agree. classify_cssc3() itself does not change, and WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • fetch_aafc_normals() reads the climate normals of Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (Derived Normal Climate Data, 5 km grid, Open Government Licence - Canada) at given points from the AAFC map service, without downloading files.
  • npdb_soil_climate() turns them into the soil climate of the book’s Tables 3 and 4: the mean annual soil temperature as the range from the air temperature to 4 degrees above it, and the climatic moisture index (growing-season precipitation over potential evapotranspiration, months of April to October above 5 degrees) with its moisture subclass. The potential evapotranspiration is computed by Thornthwaite, which matches the zones the book gives the Chernozem great groups on the NPDB, and by Hargreaves, the other end of the range.
  • npdb_dry_colour_model() fits the dry value and chroma of A horizons on their moist colour where the NPDB records both (dry value = 1.70 + 0.92 x moist value; error about one value unit), and npdb_scenario() adds the estimates to the pedons, never replacing recorded values.

On the NPDB with the 1961-1990 normals, 295 of the 899 Chernozems that waited for the climate are decided, 292 of them in their own order: agreement on the Chernozems goes from 0 to 24.1 % at the order level. The error of the dry colour seldom decides the limits between the Black, Dark Brown and Brown Chernozems (7.4 % at the great group level). The Gray Brown Luvisols go from 0 to 228 of 265 in agreement (53 decided). On the other orders, agreement goes from 90.6 to 90.1 % at the order level (56 soils of other orders are now decided as Chernozems) and from 71.9 to 74.6 % at the great group level.

soilKey 0.9.274 (2026-10-21)

Canadian classification: three readings raised by the NPDB benchmark (experimental)

classify_cssc3() changes three readings, each written down in inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml (now 58 readings). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

  • Chroma 1 or less. Clause a of the gleying test (Ch 3 key E, p. 34) counts only in materials that develop higher chromas when oxidised, which a colour cannot show: a pale calcareous C or a grey parent material is grey of its own. A horizon gleyed by clause a alone is now read with its designation: gleyed with a strong g, not gleyed when designated without one (a weak gj included; with mottles unknown, which could pass another clause, the designation decides as for unknown colours), and, with no designation, gleyed unless it holds 2 % CaCO3 or more (then undecided). The other clauses still read the colours alone. The Btg of the Luvic Gleysols reads its colours the same way.
  • Gleying and the Bt. In a soil with a Bt that begins within 50 cm, the gley colours must be in the Bt (Ch 7, p. 83: a Luvic Gleysol when they are in the Btg within 50 cm, a Gleyed Luvisol when they are only in the Aeg or below 50 cm). Soils with a solonetzic B are left out, since Ch 7 places them in the Gleysolic order by their gleying. The 10 cm minimum of Ch 7 (p. 81), which is not in the key, stays unapplied: on the NPDB it turned away 64 Gleysols the survey confirms, mostly because the depth recorded for the deepest horizon is the sampling depth.
  • Base saturation (neutral salt). Criterion 6 of the chernozemic A is read as by an unbuffered salt, as the range each horizon’s data allow: the bases over the effective CEC are the value; the bases over the bases plus the exchangeable Al are an upper bound (the H is left out); a base saturation at pH 7 is a lower bound (the unbuffered value is higher); a pH in CaCl2 of 5.5 or more (without it, 6.0 in water) places it above 80 %. Only a value known to be 80 % or less fails; the rest is undecided. Negative amounts, pH values outside 0-14 and contradictory bounds count as no data, and the KCl Al stands in for the exchangeable Al.

On the NPDB (Chernozems apart), agreement with the survey goes from 89.8 % to 90.6 % at the order level (90.5 % to 91.5 % when decided), from 70.7 % to 71.8 % at the great group level (82.1 % to 83.9 %) and from 56.3 % to 56.6 % at the subgroup level (71.3 % to 72.3 %). Decided disagreements in which the key puts a surveyed soil in the Gleysolic order fall from 317 to 178 (Luvisols 141 to 72, Brunisols 51 to 29). In turn, 32 surveyed Gleysols are now decided in the Luvisolic order, 30 of them by the Bt rule, mostly Luvic Gleysols whose Btg or Btgj does not have gley colours. Base saturation no longer decides any Chernozem outside its order (11 still fail criterion 6 because Ca is not the dominant cation): 340 Chernozems (was 445) are decided outside the order on other criteria, and 899 (was 794) wait for the soil climate.

soilKey 0.9.273 (2026-10-21)

The National Pedon Database of Canada as a benchmark (experimental)

load_npdb_pedons() reads the pre-packaged CSV files of the National Pedon Database of Canada (NPDB, version 3, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, CanSIS; Open Government Licence - Canada; not shipped with soilKey) into pedon records, with the survey’s classification under the Canadian System of Soil Classification as the reference, and benchmark_npdb() compares classify_cssc3() with it at the order, great group and subgroup levels.

The reader cleans what the files hold:

  • it rebuilds the designations in the Canadian notation;
  • it turns organic horizons recorded upward into depths above the mineral surface and repairs mineral horizons with reversed depths;
  • it reads the coded matrix colours, telling the dry colour from the moist one pedon by pedon;
  • it drops the no-data code and the copied values of total N and tells its units apart;
  • it computes base saturation from the bases and the CEC where the recorded column says something else, and swaps back a dataset’s pH columns;
  • it turns the survey’s words into the 1998 names where they name a class of the key (the Solodic subgroups as the Solonetzic ones they became).

The NPDB records no soil climate, which the key reads for the Chernozemic order and the Gray Brown Luvisols: the 1,239 Chernozems are reported apart. 794 of them are provisional; the other 445 are decided outside the order, mostly because a measured property of the A fails the chernozemic A, the most frequent being base saturation (neutral salt) of 80 % or less. On the other pedons with a reference:

Level Pedons Agreement Decided Agreement when decided
Order 7,298 89.8% 6,524 90.5%
Great group 7,272 70.7% 5,327 82.1%
Subgroup 4,041 56.3% 2,587 71.3%

Most disagreements come with a provisional result, where the records lack what the key reads: the mean annual soil temperature of the Gray Brown Luvisols (all 265 are undecided), the pH in CaCl2 of the Brunisols’ B, the organic C of the Humic Gleysols. Among the decided ones, the largest group is the gleying of the Gleysolic order: Luvisols and Brunisols with a g horizon within 50 cm, which the key places in the Gleysolic order and the survey did not.

soilKey 0.9.272 (2026-10-21)

The Canadian orders and great groups: open bottoms, other notations, climate (experimental)

classify_cssc3() reads, at the order and great-group levels, what the subgroups already read since 0.9.271:

  • the deepest horizon with no bottom depth may go on: the Bt, the podzolic B, the chernozemic A, the Brunisolic B and the Btg of the Luvic Gleysols are undecided when their thickness could change the answer, so a profile such as LFH, Ae, Bt (20 cm, no bottom) is no longer a decided Orthic Regosol;
  • the Bt is decided horizon by horizon, by its properties when they decide and otherwise by its designation: the clay increase is measured against the eluvial horizon above (Ch 2, p. 15), not against any lower-clay horizon; a horizon fails when its clay films are recorded as absent or when every clay needed shows no increase, and is undecided when the clay it should be compared with is missing; the 5 cm are then reached by adjacent Bt horizons added up, a Bt “within 50 cm” is a run that begins there, and a thin Btg on top of a Bt makes a Luvic Gleysol;
  • the podzolic B is likewise decided layer by layer, so a Bf ruled out by its chemistry no longer counts by its designation;
  • in the FAO and USDA notations a B with a t is a Bt and a Bs or Bh is podzolic B material by designation, a B with neither is not; an A, E, C or O is never podzolic B material nor a Bt; designations written in capitals (“BHS”) are read; an EB or BE is the AB of a Solod; an E is the Ae of the Chernozemic and Solonetzic tests, so a Chernozem described as A, Bw, Bk, C reaches the Chernozemic order;
  • the word “and” of a split horizon (“Ae and Bt”) no longer switches the Canadian notation off;
  • the soil moisture subclass is read whatever its spelling (“Sub-humid”, “semi-arid”).

In about 3,000 test profiles, 88 change order or great group: 82 described in another notation with a Bt, now a provisional Luvisol or Luvic Gleysol instead of a Regosol or Gleysol, and 6 whose designated Bt shows no clay increase over the eluvial horizon above, now ruled out by that measured clay. In Canadian-notation profiles the subgroups and great groups can also change where clay films are recorded as absent, where clay was given on an organic layer, or where the eluvial horizon has no clay recorded (the designation then decides). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.271 (2026-10-21)

The Canadian subgroups: Solonetzic, Chernozemic and Luvisolic (experimental)

classify_cssc3() now keys the subgroups of the last three orders of the Canadian System of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3, pp. 42-49), 101 more, so all 231 subgroups are keyed and the name goes down to the subgroup in every order (“Dark Gray Solod”, “Calcareous Black Chernozem”, “Gleyed Brunisolic Gray Luvisol”). The subgroups read, as before, measured properties first and the Canadian designations second:

  • Solonetzic: the dry colour value of the A (Brown, Dark Brown, Black, and Gray and Dark Gray with a low chroma and a subhumid climate in the Solods and Solodized Solonetz), a strongly alkaline A (pH above 8.5), faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm;
  • Chernozemic: a slickenside horizon, a weak solonetzic B (Bnj, Bnjtj, Btnj), eluvial horizons of 2 cm, a Bmk of 5 cm (0.5 % CaCO3 or more, or a k), no B of 5 cm, faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm;
  • Luvisolic: a slickenside horizon, a fragipan, a podzolic B over a Bt within 50 cm, a Bm of chroma 3 or a thin Bf in the upper solum, an Ah of 5 cm, a Btnj, distinct mottles within 50 cm or prominent ones at 50-100 cm.

The Solonetzic great groups have no residual subgroup in the key, so a Solonetzic soil without an A stops at the great group; where an LFH lies directly over an Ae, the Gray subgroups read the Ae, as Ch 12 words them. The colour of the A is read over the whole A: a horizon with no value leaves the class undecided when it could change it. The readings where the book is silent are added to inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml (now 57). The Solonetzic example of make_cssc3_example() gains a dry colour and a pH, so it keys to a Dark Brown Solonetz.

Two changes reach the subgroups keyed since 0.9.269: a horizon with no bottom depth (the deepest one, which may go on) no longer counts as 0 cm when horizons are added up towards a thickness, so the Rego and Eluviated subgroups are undecided instead of decided on it; and a buried Aeb is no longer the Ae of the Eluviated Brunisols. Orders and great groups do not change, and WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.270 (2026-10-21)

The Canadian subgroups: Podzolic, Gleysolic, Brunisolic and Regosolic (experimental)

classify_cssc3() now keys the subgroups of four more orders of the Canadian System of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3, pp. 40-51), 67 more, 130 of the 231 in all, so the name goes down to the subgroup in seven orders (“Ortstein Humo-Ferric Podzol”, “Fera Humic Gleysol”, “Gleyed Eluviated Dystric Brunisol”, “Cumulic Regosol”); the Solonetzic, Chernozemic and Luvisolic orders still stop at the great group. The subgroups read, as before, measured properties first and the Canadian designations second:

  • Podzolic: an ortstein (no depth limit), placic and duric horizons and a fragipan within the control section (cementation class, or a c in the designation), a deep Bt, an Ah of 10 cm, distinct to prominent mottles within 1 m;
  • Gleysolic: a slickenside horizon, a solonetzic B, a fragipan below the Btg, the Humic Gleysol A, a Bgf horizon (dithionite Fe over the parent material, or gf), no B of 10 cm;
  • Brunisolic: a duric horizon, an Ae or Aej of 2 cm, gleying mottles within 50 cm or at 50-100 cm;
  • Regosolic: cumulic layering (colour value, organic C with depth, or a buried A) and faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm.

The readings where the book is silent are added to inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml (now 54). The Vertic Solonetz great group now reads its slickenside horizon horizon by horizon, as the Vertic Gleysol subgroups do: a horizon with no designation and no slickenside record is undecided instead of ‘none’, and a designation in the FAO or USDA notation is read (an ss counts, a designation without ss fails). The surface A of the great groups no longer takes in a buried A (b) under it, so an Ah over an Ahb is measured by the Ah alone. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

soilKey 0.9.269 (2026-10-21)

The Canadian subgroups: Cryosolic, Organic and Vertisolic (experimental)

classify_cssc3() now keys the subgroups of three orders of the Canadian System of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3, pp. 37-40), 63 of the 231, so the name goes down to the subgroup there (“Terric Humic Mesisol”, “Brunisolic Dystric Turbic Cryosol”, “Gleyed Vertisol”); the other orders still stop at the great group. The subgroups read, as the orders and great groups do, measured properties first and the Canadian designations second:

  • Cryosolic: ice layers, the mineral contact and the peat above it, the dominant peat below 40 cm, gleying, organic horizons over 15 cm, the pH of the B horizons, the thickness of the Bm, a Bt under an eluvial horizon;
  • Organic: O horizons under folic ones, woody material, the dominant folic horizon, hydric, terric, limnic and cumulic layers, and the thickness of each kind of peat;
  • Vertisolic: prominent, or faint to distinct, mottles within 50 cm.

The readings where the book is silent are added to inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml (now 46). The Cryosolic example pedon gains pH values. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

Fixes to the orders and great groups of 0.9.267 and 0.9.268:

  • the Organic great groups leave limnic and folic layers out of the peat tally (they are neither fibric, mesic nor humic); a limnic layer is not a terric contact, and a middle tier of limnic material only is read with the surface tier;
  • gleying (Gleysolic order) is decided horizon by horizon: a horizon’s measured colours outrank its own g, and a horizon with no colours and no designation is undecided instead of ‘not gleyed’;
  • the rows are read in depth order whatever the order they are given in (on a copy; the layer numbers of the trace follow that order);
  • the thick-A rule of the gleying test reads the whole surface A (adjacent Ah and Ap from the mineral surface; a buried A, b, never counts) and tests the mineral horizon right below it, whatever it is, a gap in the record allowed; in another notation the A masters are left out of the test and the E masters as the Ae are (a thick, deep E is tested);
  • a horizon with no bottom depth ends where the next one down begins, and the deepest one may go on (both options of the Organic order, the organic column and the peat tally read it as possibly deep);
  • limnic layers are read from whole words of their recorded origin, not on rock, and from the L master of the FAO and USDA notations;
  • in designations of another notation, W and R are never mineral horizons, and an O or H without organic C is organic.

soilKey 0.9.268 (2026-10-21)

The Canadian great groups (experimental)

classify_cssc3() now keys the 31 great groups of the Canadian System of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Great Groups, Ch 3, pp. 35-36), under the ten orders of 0.9.267, so the name is the great group (“Humo-Ferric Podzol”, “Dark Brown Chernozem”) and the order is in rsg_or_order. The great groups read, as the orders do, measured properties first and the Canadian designations second:

  • Cryosolic: organic material over permafrost, cryoturbation (y);
  • Organic: the folic thickness of Ch 9 (L, F, H), the dominant material of the middle tier (fibric, mesic or humic, by rubbed fibre, then designation), widened to the surface tier only by a terric, lithic or hydric layer;
  • Vertisolic: surface dry value or Ah thickness, by drainage class, and the Ch 13 rule for the Ap of a poorly drained cultivated soil;
  • Podzolic: at least 10 cm of Bh or Bhf chemistry;
  • Gleysolic: a gleyed Bt (Btg), a humic Ah or Ap with at least 2 % organic C;
  • Solonetzic: a slickenside horizon, an Ae of at least 2 cm, an AB or BA;
  • Chernozemic: the dry value and chroma of the chernozemic A and signs of eluviation;
  • Luvisolic: a forest mull Ah and a mean annual soil temperature of 8 C;
  • Brunisolic: a thick dark Ah or Ap and the pH (CaCl2) of the upper B;
  • Regosolic: an Ah or Ap of 10 cm.

The last great group of each order is the key’s “other soils”. The readings where the book is silent are added to inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml (now 33). The per-layer readings of podzolic B chemistry and of gley colours are factored out of the order diagnostics without changing them. The example pedons now reach a great group each. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

Fixes to the 0.9.267 order key, all in the Organic order:

  • a folic layer (L, F, H) lying on peat is read as litter over peat, so F 0-5 cm over Om 5-160 cm is an Organic soil (it was keyed as Regosolic); the litter is not counted towards the peat limits;
  • the kind of the surface organic layer is read from measured rubbed fibre before its designation (an Om with 60 % rubbed fibre is fibric);
  • a layer of unknown organic status leaves the order undecided where it could change the answer, instead of failing it;
  • in designations of another notation, the masters A, B, C and E are read as mineral, R as rock and W as water when organic C is missing.

soilKey 0.9.267 (2026-10-20)

The Canadian System of Soil Classification, to the order (experimental)

The first national system on the registry: classify_cssc3() keys a profile through the Key to Soil Orders of the Canadian System of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Soil Classification Working Group 1998, Ch 3, pp. 33-34), from Cryosolic to Regosolic. Great groups and subgroups follow in later releases, so the name is the order. The system is experimental and opt-in: classify_all() and the Pro app keep running WRB, SiBCS and USDA by default; classify_all(systems = c("wrb2022", "sibcs5", "usda", "cssc3")) runs it beside them, and classify_cssc3() alone.

The Canadian keys are written largely in terms of horizon designations, which Chapter 2 defines partly by measurable properties. Each diagnostic reads the measured properties first (podzolic B chemistry, the Bt clay increase with clay films, the solonetzic B Ca/Na ratio, the chernozemic A, the gley colours) and the designations second, in the Canadian notation, where f is an illuvial Fe-Al-organic accumulation, m a slightly altered B, v a vertic horizon, ss slickensides, y cryoturbation, z permafrost and j a weak expression of the suffix before it. Measured properties decide whenever they can, pass or fail; designations decide only what they leave open, and only when the profile’s notation is Canadian (declared in site$designation_system, a Canadian site, or no sign of the FAO/USDA notation), because the same letters mean other things there. The trace records which route decided, and a warning says when the order rests on designations alone. The chernozemic A includes a soil-climate criterion (mean annual soil temperature at least 0 C, moisture subclass drier than humid), read from the new site fields mean_annual_soil_temp_C and soil_moisture_subclass or approximated from the USDA regimes; without it, the orders keyed after Chernozemic are reported as provisional. The choices where the book is silent are listed in inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml.

Three horizon attributes are added for the Canadian key and read by no other: fe_pyro_pct and al_pyro_pct (sodium-pyrophosphate-extractable Fe and Al) and mottle_contrast (faint, distinct, prominent). make_cssc3_example() builds one example profile per order. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change: the 44 canonical fixtures are identical.

soilKey 0.9.266 (2026-10-20)

One file of metadata for the horizon attributes

The section, unit and description of each of the 112 canonical horizon columns now live in inst/schemas/horizon-attributes.yaml, and the new horizon_attribute_spec() returns them as a table with each column’s type and accepted aliases. The file also has room for what the national systems will need: the keys that read an attribute, the values of a categorical one and the range of a numeric one. The attribute reference inst/ATTRIBUTES.md is generated from it (before, the generator parsed the comments of R/utils.R and kept its own table of units), and a test fails when the file and the reference fall out of step. The reference’s tables are unchanged. No classification changes.

soilKey 0.9.265 (2026-10-20)

A generic classifier for ordered keys

Most of the national systems on the roadmap (Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Hungary, China) are ordered keys of the USDA kind: at each level the first class whose tests pass is assigned. Their classifiers will be thin wrappers around a new internal engine, classify_hierarchical(), that walks the levels named in the system’s registry entry. Two rules differ from the three older keys, on purpose: a class is assigned only when its tests pass (a default: true entry passes by definition), so a level where nothing passes stays unassigned instead of falling back to the last class of its list (with a warning saying where the name stopped); and a class that could not be decided for lack of data, tested before the one assigned, makes the assignment provisional. Run on the USDA rules, it gives the same name, order and evidence grade as classify_usda() for all 44 canonical fixtures.

ClassificationResult gains three fields: system_id (the registry id; WRB, SiBCS, USDA and SmartSolos results now carry it), levels (the class assigned at each level) and provisional_because. Its print() counts the classes actually tested (for SiBCS and USDA it counted the phases of the nested trace) and calls them RSGs only for WRB. No classification changes.

soilKey 0.9.264 (2026-10-20)

The rule engine reads nested blocks and none_of

National keys say things such as “other soils that have A, and B or C, and not D”. The rule engine now reads that in YAML: an entry of an all_of, any_of or none_of list may itself be one of these blocks, and none_of (no test may pass) joins all_of and any_of, with the same three-valued logic (an undecided test leaves the block undecided unless the outcome is already settled). A nested block appears in the key trace as a test of its own, with its sub-results as evidence.

The lower levels of a key are now read from the folders that the system’s registry entry names (great_groups from great-groups/), not from a fixed list of six folder names. The rule validator also reports blocks that name more than one combinator (the engine reads only one of them), combinators written as a mapping instead of a list, class codes and names that are not quoted strings (YAML reads an unquoted N as a logical and 11 as a number), codes listed twice in one list or one level, and, for systems added after the registry, predicates without the system’s suffix, so that a Canadian Chernozemic gate can never be WRB’s chernozem(). The helpers that every key shares (evidence grade, ambiguities, missing attributes) move from R/key-wrb2022.R to R/key-common.R, unchanged.

No result changes: the 44 canonical fixtures give identical names, key traces, evidence grades and warnings, and no rule of the three systems nests, mixes combinators or uses none_of.

soilKey 0.9.263 (2026-10-20)

A registry of classification systems

Each classification system is now a folder inst/rules/<id>/ holding its key and a system.yaml entry: id, aliases, classifier, levels, display names, edition, citation and status. load_rules(), classify_all() and the rule validator read that registry instead of repeating the three ids, and the new soilkey_systems() lists it. This is the first step towards the national systems (Canada, Australia, New Zealand and others): a new system will be added by adding its folder.

Nothing else changes. The 44 canonical fixtures give the same names, key traces, evidence grades and warnings as in 0.9.262, and every id or alias accepted so far still works, including the partial ones such as "wrb". classify_all(systems = "sibcs5") is now accepted as well as "sibcs". load_rules() now writes its default as "wrb2022"; it was the vector of the three ids, of which the first was used.

soilKey 0.9.262 (2026-10-15)

The WRB 2022 reference points to the 2022 edition

The README and the Portuguese getting-started vignette gave, for WRB 2022 (IUSS Working Group WRB, 4th edition), an FAO OpenKnowledge PDF that is the 2014 edition: its own title reads “World reference base for soil resources 2014”. Both now give the 2022 edition at ISRIC, https://files.isric.org/public/documents/WRB_fourth_edition_2022-12-18.pdf. The classification keys do not change.

soilKey 0.9.261 (2026-10-14)

Pro app: a visitor counter in the footer

The footer of the hosted app (soilkeypro.com) says, in one line, how many people are on the site now, how many have visited and from how many countries; a click on the countries opens a map of them above the footer. Asked for by the maintainer.

  • A person is counted once. On the first visit the browser keeps a mark in its own storage (no identifier) and tells the server it is a new visitor; a later visit from the same browser counts as a session only. Nothing that identifies the visitor is sent or kept.

  • The country comes from the address of the request, looked up in DB-IP’s IP to Country Lite table (CC BY 4.0), which the image downloads when it is built and the footer credits. The address is read for that and kept nowhere.

  • Not counted: automated browsers (headless Chrome, crawlers, command-line clients, the capacity test, the Claude app’s browser), and pages that never open a Shiny session.

  • The numbers are kept in Firestore, in the app’s own Google Cloud project: one document of totals (visitors, sessions, visitors by country, the day counting began) and one document per running instance with how many sessions it holds, written every 30 s. “Online now” adds up the instances that wrote in the last 90 s. Only soilkeypro.com writes to these; a tagged revision writes to separate test collections, and a local run to none.

  • Before the counter, the request logs of Cloud Run (30 days) are read once by deploy/cloudrun/visitors-backfill.R: a session is a request to /websocket/ answered with 101, a visitor a distinct address. The logs begin on 2026-10-07, when the site came back online.

  • The map waits for a click. The footer is on screen in every tab, and a map in it (190 px in all) took the height the tabs’ own tables need: with a 790 px window the key trace of Classify had none left, and DT does not draw a table of height 0. The map now opens in a panel above the line’s “from N countries” button (below it when there is no room above) and closes on a second click, a click elsewhere, Escape or, on a phone, a scroll of the page; the footer grows by one line only. On a phone the map keeps its 210 px (the app’s narrow-screen rule sets every map’s height to “auto”).

  • Classify’s key trace is drawn at its own height, not the height left over in its card (DTOutput(fill = FALSE)). With a short window, or a footer one line taller, it was 36 px or less before.

New files: R/utils_visitors.R and R/mod_visitors.R in the app, its country table data/countries.csv (built by data-raw/visitor_countries.R; see inst/DATA-PROVENANCE.md), the image step in deploy/fly/Dockerfile, and eight strings in each language. The classification keys do not change.

soilKey 0.9.260 (2026-10-14)

Pro app: the light base map is Esri’s; CARTO’s asks for a key

CARTO’s base maps now answer a request without an API key with a tile that says “API KEY REQUIRED”. The app used CARTO’s light map, “Positron”, as the base of the Batch and Grid maps and as the “Light” choice of the Map tab, so those showed the notice in place of a map. The checks of each release counted the tiles that loaded, not what they showed, and did not see it.

The light map is now Esri’s light gray canvas (Esri.WorldGrayCanvas), with its attribution, in the three places and in the list the app registers its map scripts from. The Map tab’s choice reads “Light (Esri)”. Nothing else changes.

soilKey 0.9.259 (2026-10-14)

CRAN release: 2026-10-14

Tests: the slow ones run off CRAN

The CRAN pre-test of 0.9.258 (2026-10-14) did not pass automatically on r-devel-windows-x86_64: “Overall checktime 14 min > 10 min”, mainly from the tests, 461 s on Windows (158 s on Debian). The CRAN team asked to reduce the test timings, among other ways by running less important tests only off CRAN.

Every test that took more than 0.03 s on CRAN’s terms (NOT_CRAN unset, the installed package) on a fast machine now starts with skip_on_cran(): 457 tests in 137 files. They run as before with devtools::test() and wherever NOT_CRAN=true. The core of the three keys stays on CRAN, slow as it is: the tests that the canonical profiles classify to their WRB Reference Soil Group, to their SiBCS order, and to their USDA order.

soilKey 0.9.257 (2026-10-13)

SiBCS key: the activity of the clay and the base saturation in the larger part of the first 100 cm of the B

The key gives the Luvissolos a “horizonte B textural com argila de atividade alta e saturação por bases alta na maior parte dos primeiros 100 cm do horizonte B (inclusive BA)” (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 4, p. 113), asks the same section of the Nitossolos (p. 114), and the definitions of the classes of the lower levels repeat it. Cap. 1 (p. 30) takes the activity of the clay “no horizonte B (inclusive BA e exclusive BC) ou no horizonte C (inclusive CA), quando não existe B”, and does not apply it to “materiais de solo das classes texturais areia e areia franca”.

atividade_argila_alta() and eutrofico() passed with one layer of B or of C, anywhere in the profile:

  • the C of a profile, with little clay and a high ratio of CEC to clay, made the clay of the whole profile one of high activity;
  • one eutrophic layer, the C as often as not, made the profile eutrophic;
  • the two did not have to be found in the same part of the profile.

With both, an Argissolo with a B of low base saturation keyed Luvissolos (AC 10374, an Argissolo Álico of high activity: B1, B2 and B3 with V of 49, 40 and 37%, and a C with 76%). The same reading kept a B nítico from being one, as it asks for clay of low activity, and sent to the Luvissolos the Nitossolos that come after them in the key. Of the 260 complete profiles keyed Luvissolos in the default mode, 86 had that reference.

Now, in a profile with a B horizon:

  • The section is the first 100 cm of the B: the B layers, the BA with them and the BC not, that begin within 100 cm of the top of the uppermost one, each with the thickness it has inside the section.
  • The activity is high, or the base saturation is, when the layers where it is so make more than half of the thickness of the section, among the layers that say. Half is not the larger part. A layer with no CEC, no clay or no V recorded is left out of both sides of the count.
  • A layer of areia or of areia franca is left out of the activity. It is told by its sand, silt and clay. It was told by a clay under 15%, which also left out the franco-arenosa and the franca with little clay.

A profile with no B is read as before, in its C layers. The sections that the book gives for those classes, each its own (Gleissolos: “dentro de 100 cm a partir da superfície”), are not in this version.

The two functions are read by the Chernossolos and Luvissolos steps, by the B nítico, and by the classes of the third level (Eutróficos, Distróficos, Ta, Tb) of every order, which follow the same section.

soilKey 0.9.256 (2026-10-13)

SiBCS key: more marks of the older notation of horizons

Since 0.9.250 the “A2” of a profile written in the notation in use until 1988 is read as the E of today, and its “B3” as the BC. The profile was known to be in that notation by a B followed at once by a number (“B1”, “B21t”) or by a “(B)”. A podzol described “A1, A21, A22, Bhir” has neither: its A2 was read as a part of the A, and with no E above it its Bhir was no B espódico by item (a) of the book (0.9.255).

Decided on 2026-10-13: three more marks.

  • An A or a C followed at once by two figures (“A11”, “A12”, “A21”, “C11”). The older notation numbers the parts of a horizon after the figure of the horizon; the present one counts them from 1 after the letters.
  • The suffix “ir” in a B (“Bir”, “Bhir”, “B2ir”), the illuvial iron that is written “s” today.
  • The suffix “pl” in a B or a C (“Bpl”, “B21pl”, “Cpl”), the plinthite that is written “f” today.

The suffix “cn” of the concretions is not a mark. It was measured with the other three and is found in profiles otherwise written in the present notation: GO 12592, a Latossolo Vermelho described “A1, A2, AB, BA, Bw1, Bw2, BC, C1, Ccn, C2”, whose A2 has 43% of clay and 1.6% of organic carbon and is the second part of the A, would have had it read as an E and left its order.

Like the correspondence of the A2 and of the B3 itself, these marks are not in SiBCS 2018, which gives the present notation only.

Measured

soilKey 0.9.255 (2026-10-13)

SiBCS key: item (a) of the B espódico

The B espódico (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 62-65) is a horizon “com acumulação iluvial de compostos organometálicos” that has one or more of three characteristics, the first being “a) Um horizonte E (álbico ou não) sobrejacente e cores úmidas de acordo com um dos itens a seguir: 1) Matiz 5YR ou mais vermelho; 2) Matiz 7,5YR com valor 5 ou menor e croma 4 ou menor; 3) Matiz 10YR, com valor e croma 3 ou menor; 4) Cores neutras com valor 3 ou menor (N 3/)”.

B_espodico() was the spodic horizon of the WRB, which asks for aluminium and iron by oxalate, or for a horizon named Bh or Bs under an albic one. The items of the book were not tested. The sheets of the Brazilian surveys seldom have the oxalate extraction: of the 98 Espodossolos of the BDsolos export the default mode keyed 4 as such.

The colours of the item cannot stand alone. “5YR ou mais vermelho” is the colour of the B textural of many an Argissolo that lies below an E, and the Espodossolos come before the Argissolos in the key; what tells the two apart is the illuvial accumulation of the heading, which the sheets do not measure. Three ways of asking for it were measured on the 389 profiles with an E:

the B, below an E and with a colour of the item, has default mode morphological mode
0.5% of organic carbon or more and a pH under 5.9, the limits of the WRB, which the book cites as its source 19 reach their reference, 17 leave it 0 and 18
0.5% or more and at least twice that of the E 18 and 2 1 and 2
the same, with no cerosidade recorded 18 and 0 1 and 0

Decided on 2026-10-13: the third. Where the WRB test does not find the horizon, a B layer of 2.5 cm or more is a B espódico when

  • an E lies above it;
  • its moist colour is one of the four of item (a);
  • its organic carbon is 0.5% or more and at least twice that of the nearest E above it, the form the book gives in item (b)(3) for aluminium and iron by oxalate (“valor 0,50 ou maior, sendo este valor pelo menos o dobro do encontrado no horizonte sobrejacente”); and
  • no cerosidade is recorded in it, which is the mark of illuvial clay.

This is a reading by analogy, not the letter of the book. It is so stated in the documentation of the function. Items (b) and (c), the cementation and the ortstein, are not tested. The reading is the same in both modes; the morphological mode goes on reading the designation as well.

soilKey 0.9.254 (2026-10-13)

SiBCS key: an O or H layer recorded upward from the mineral soil is part of the histic horizon

The older descriptions give the organic layers that lie on a mineral soil upward from its top: “O 120-0”, or “Hd 110-60” above “Hoj 60-0”, over a “Cg 0-10”. With an upper depth greater than the lower one, such a layer had a thickness below zero and was never part of the horizonte hístico. BDsolos RJ 14357, an Organossolo Háplico whose one layer is “O 120-0” with 17% of organic carbon, keyed Neossolos.

Decided on 2026-10-13: the layer is counted.

  • In horizonte_histico() an O or H layer whose upper depth is greater than its lower one lies above the mineral surface, with the thickness between its two figures; layers so recorded adjoin one another and the mineral soil as they are written.
  • The 80 cm of the Organossolos step (0.9.253) are counted from the surface of the soil, the top of the uppermost of those layers.
  • The depths of the profile are not changed, and no other test reads them this way. A layer that is no O or H is not read upward: a mineral horizon with its depths the wrong way round is a slip of the sheet.
